analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license and safety training to own a gun, bans assault weapons and silencers, and funds violence prevention.
analysis.headline: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill with three Democratic cosponsors in December 2023; the Senate Finance Committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every person buying or owning a firearm or ammunition to get a federal license, which means passing a written and hands-on safety test, a background check, and being at least 21. It would require background checks on nearly all gun sales, add a seven-business-day waiting period, ban assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, ban silencers, raise taxes on gun sales, and fund community violence intervention and gun violence research. It would also let courts temporarily take guns away from people judged to be a danger to themselves or others, and tighten rules on domestic abusers, stalkers, and gun dealers.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities affected by gun violence, victims of domestic violence and stalking, and families at risk of gun suicide gain new legal protections: licensing with safety training, waiting periods, secure-storage rules, extreme risk protection orders, and domestic violence loopholes closed [S2]. Community organizations gain a new grant program, and researchers gain dedicated funding [S2]. People who already lawfully own guns keep them under a grandfather exception and could qualify for a 10-year license [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to gun violence and domestic abuse

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal firearm owner's license requiring the applicant to be 21, pass written and hands-on safety testing, and clear a background check; licenses last 10 years [S2].

Requires background checks for essentially all firearm transfers, with exceptions for certain family gifts, inheritances, and temporary transfers like hunting, and extends the waiting period before a sale completes to 7 business days [S2].
Bans assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition feeding devices, bans firearm silencers, bans untraceable and undetectable firearms, and funds buy-back programs for grandfathered weapons [S2].

Expands federal prohibitions to cover misdemeanor stalking convictions and more domestic violence protection orders, and closes the 'boyfriend loophole' by broadening the definition of intimate partner to include dating partners [S2].

Lets family members and law enforcement petition a federal court for an extreme risk protection order to temporarily remove firearms from someone posing a danger, with due-process hearings, and funds state red-flag programs [S2].

Raises the minimum purchase age for any firearm or ammunition to 21, requires secure storage with penalties if a minor or prohibited person gets an unsecured gun, extends gun-free school zones to colleges, and directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set safety standards for gun locks and safes [S2].

Repeals the legal shield protecting gun manufacturers and dealers from many civil lawsuits, makes gun trace data usable in civil cases, increases excise taxes on firearms, and subjects guns to consumer product safety jurisdiction [S2].
Authorizes community violence intervention grants and dedicated funding for research on gun violence prevention [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Gun buyers and owners bear new costs and delays: license applications with training and testing, a 7-business-day waiting period, secure-storage duties with civil fines and possible criminal penalties, and a ban on acquiring new assault weapons or silencers [S2]. Firearms manufacturers, dealers, and silencer makers bear higher excise taxes, mandatory dealer inspections and employee background checks, record-keeping requirements, and exposure to civil lawsuits after the liability shield is repealed [S2]. Taxpayers fund the licensing system, red-flag grant program, and community violence grants [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun buyers, owners, and the firearms industry

drawbacks.text: The licensing system is a real burden on gun owners: a written and live-fire test, background investigation, photo, and annual re-checks are required, and possession without a license carries up to 2 years in prison [S2].

The 'unsuitability' standard for denying or revoking a license rests on a preponderance of evidence that someone 'could potentially create a risk' to public safety, a broad standard that critics would say gives officials wide discretion even with the court hearing and appeal rights the bill provides [S2].

The 7-business-day waiting period and the 21 minimum age delay purchases even for buyers who clear every check, including younger adults who may hunt or work on farms, though the bill carves out supervised exceptions for those uses [S2].
Grandfathered assault weapon owners keep their guns but face background-checked transfers only, and buy-backs are voluntary, so the ban does not remove weapons already in circulation [S2].

Enforcement depends on large new administrative systems at the Justice Department, a license-verification database, and dealer inspections, whose cost and implementation burden the bill authorizes but does not cap [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pursues gun violence reduction through the most comprehensive package in this Congress: licensing, universal background checks, waiting periods, an assault weapon and silencer ban, red-flag orders, domestic violence fixes, industry accountability, and funded prevention programs [S2]. The benefits would fall on everyone exposed to gun violence; the costs fall heavily on gun owners and the gun industry, and the license standard's breadth is the most serious design concern an honest supporter would acknowledge. As written it is sweeping, and its fate suggests the votes were never there; no compromise version was ever considered in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or voted, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced S. 3407, the Gun Violence Prevention and Community Safety Act of 2023, in the Senate on December 5, 2023, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Booker, Markey, and Hirono [S1][S2][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S4].
The bill's cosponsor page lists 3 Democratic cosponsors [S3].
No further action was ever recorded: no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll-call vote, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers, dealers, and silencer makers are better off: no license requirement, background check expansion, excise tax increase, or repeal of their lawsuit protection ever took effect, and current law on gun ownership stayed as it was.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it; it was read twice and referred to the Finance Committee

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so the record shows no partisan split; all four sponsors were Democrats and the bill never left a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would impose a licensing requirement on their customers, universal background checks, dealer inspections, employee background checks, and higher excise taxes, and would repeal the federal shield that limits many civil suits against them. It would also ban sales of assault weapons, large-capacity magazines, and silencers, shrinking their market.
Title V bans firearm silencers and mufflers outright and restricts certain accessories, ending that product line, with buy-back programs for existing items.

industries.industry: Gun lock and gun safe manufacturers
industries.note: The bill requires secure storage and directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set mandatory safety standards for locks and safes, creating demand for certified products.
A new grant program would fund community-based violence intervention work, and a separate funding stream would support gun violence research.
